criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Determine whether every dimension in the taxonomy captures a fundamentally different type of distinction. If two dimensions are really just different values on the same underlying axis (for example 'Bug Reports' and 'Feature Requests' are both values of 'Issue Type'), the taxonomy fails this criterion.
criteria.reason: The output defines multiple taxonomy dimensions (e.g., “Consistency and Replication Model Choice” with strong/consensus vs WAL eventual truth; “Underlying Storage Substrate Strategy”; “Scaling Tradeoff Framing and Constraints”; etc.), but the evaluation steps require verifying that each dimension is a distinct axis relative to the input and that no two dimensions collapse onto the same underlying axis. Here, several dimensions overlap in underlying meaning: “Scaling Tradeoff Framing and Constraints” includes correctness/consistency and latency drivers that are tightly coupled to “Consistency and Replication Model Choice,” and “Underlying Storage Substrate Strategy” includes WAL-backed truth which is essentially the same distinction as the WAL-driven eventual truth value in dimension 1. Additionally, “Reliability and Operations Philosophy (Pets vs Cattle)” and “Replica Maintenance and Compaction Placement” both describe operational placement/management of replicas, which risks collapsing into the same underlying axis of operational management. Because these overlaps are not clearly separated into non-overlapping axes, the non-overlapping requirement is not satisfied.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Determine whether the dimension names and descriptions are clear enough that a labeler could classify documents accurately without ambiguity, and whether each description explains what kind of documents fall along that dimension.
criteria.reason: The evaluation steps require comparing dimension names and descriptions between the Input and the Actual Output to check for matching/clear classification criteria. However, the provided Input only says to “Generate the taxonomy that can be used to label the user intent in the conversation” and does not include any dimension names or classification guidance. As a result, there is nothing to compare against the Actual Output’s dimensions (e.g., “Consistency and Replication Model Choice,” “Underlying Storage Substrate Strategy,” etc.), so the required checks for equivalence, boundary alignment, and explicit include/exclude criteria cannot be performed.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: Determine whether the taxonomy captures all major axes of variation implied by the stated use case, or whether recurring kinds of distinctions are missing. Judge against the use case in the input, not against topics the use case excludes.
criteria.reason: The input asks for a taxonomy to label user intent in a conversation, but the actual output provides a domain-specific architecture taxonomy focused on Git/repository replication, storage substrate, and scaling tradeoffs (e.g., “Consistency and Replication Model Choice,” “Underlying Storage Substrate Strategy,” “Replica Maintenance and Compaction Placement”). This does not directly match the stated use case of labeling user intent, so the major axes of variation implied by “user intent” (e.g., question vs request vs clarification, topic selection, action type) are not represented. However, the output does show strong internal coverage of recurring technical distinction types (consistency model variants like strong/consensus vs WAL eventual truth; substrate options like S3-backed WAL vs client-side virtualization; and operational placement like primary-only compaction), and it includes multiple alternatives evaluated and constraints framing. The main shortcoming is the mismatch between the input’s intent-labeling goal and the actual output’s technical taxonomy.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Determine whether every dimension serves the stated use case. Dimensions that exist in the abstract but do not help achieve the use case in the input should lower the score.
criteria.reason: The input asks for a taxonomy to label user intent in a conversation, but the actual output provides architecture/replication/storage taxonomy dimensions (e.g., “Consistency and Replication Model Choice,” “Underlying Storage Substrate Strategy,” “Reliability and Operations Philosophy”). None of the listed dimensions are directly justified as user-intent labels, and the output includes many abstract technical dimensions that do not support the stated use case. Because the dimensions do not align with conversational intent labeling, the coverage of the input’s use case is effectively absent.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: Determine whether the taxonomy contains an 'Other', 'Miscellaneous', or similarly vague catch-all dimension, or whether every dimension is specific enough that a document clearly belongs or does not belong.
criteria.reason: The input asks to generate a taxonomy for labeling user intent, but it does not provide any taxonomy dimensions to compare against. The actual output introduces multiple specific dimensions (e.g., “Consistency and Replication Model Choice,” “Underlying Storage Substrate Strategy,” “Scaling Tradeoff Framing and Constraints”) and does not include any catch-all category like “Other/Miscellaneous.” Because the input taxonomy is missing, the evaluation steps about preserving or introducing a catch-all category cannot be properly verified; however, the output remains specific and does not add an unnecessary vague category, which partially aligns with the specificity check.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Determine whether each dimension is truly an axis of variation rather than a single value dressed up as an axis. A dimension named 'Bug Reports' might really be one value on an 'Issue Type' axis that also includes feature requests and questions.
criteria.reason: The response defines multiple dimensions (e.g., “Consistency and Replication Model Choice”, “Underlying Storage Substrate Strategy”, “Scaling Tradeoff Framing and Constraints”, etc.) and each includes several distinct values, satisfying the requirement that dimensions represent true axes of variation rather than single fixed values. For matching dimension names, the output treats them as categories with multiple alternatives (e.g., strong/consensus vs WAL-driven eventual truth vs relaxed consensus; multiple substrate strategies like Spokes, distributed object store, S3-backed WAL, client-side virtualization). It also avoids collapsing re-labeled single values into one option, and instead expands them into alternatives. However, the input only asks to “Generate the taxonomy that can be used to label the user intent in the conversation,” which is broad and not explicitly tied to the specific axes shown; the output therefore may be over-specific and not fully grounded in the stated “user intent” labeling requirement, though it still follows the axis/alternatives structure well.

criteria.name: Dimensional coverage
criteria.description: Determine whether every document in the input can be placed along at least one dimension of the taxonomy. Penalize documents that fit no dimension's axis of variation, naming the document themes that are left uncovered.
criteria.reason: The response provides a taxonomy-like mapping with multiple dimensions (e.g., consistency/replication model choice, underlying storage substrate strategy, compaction placement, pets vs cattle). However, it does not follow the evaluation steps because it never maps the actual Input documents to the taxonomy dimensions/axes in a way that can be verified: the Input documents are unlabeled with IDs, while the Actual Output references opaque supporting_doc_ids that do not correspond to any visible Input identifiers. As a result, it is impossible to confirm that every Input document is assigned to at least one dimension, and the required coverage check (flagging any unmapped documents and listing their themes and uncovered dimensions) cannot be performed. Additionally, several major Input themes appear only indirectly (e.g., AI agents as workload forcing function, Git client intolerance of eventual consistency, evolution timeline), but there is no explicit per-document mapping to demonstrate coverage.
